bolton_2006_cake_complete_blocking.name: Cake-complete blocking
bolton_2006_cake_complete_blocking.description: The paper develops five combined fouling models for membrane filtration, including a cake-complete model for protein solutions filtered through microporous membranes. The model represents fouling through both growth of a cake layer and loss of open membrane area, and predicts permeate volume over time at constant pressure or pressure over time at constant flow. It uses Darcy’s law and two fitted parameters, and approaches the individual cake or complete-blocking models when one mechanism dominates. The authors tested it using sterile filtration of human plasma IgG and virus filtration of BSA, as well as constant-flow IgG tests, in bench-scale membrane holders. They compared its fits with individual and other combined fouling models and considered its use for membrane-area sizing.

facts.quote: The combined models were assessed through testing under constant pressure and constant flow modes with solutions of bovine serum albumin and human IgG.

facts.text: The experimental streams were BSA for virus filtration and human plasma IgG for sterile filtration.
facts.quote: Bovine serum albumin was filtered through virus retention membranes and human IgG was filtered through sterilizing grade microporous membranes.

facts.text: Complete blocking represents particles sealing pore entrances so those pores no longer carry flow.
facts.quote: Complete blocking assumes that particles seal off pore entrances and prevent flow.

facts.text: Cake filtration represents particles accumulating on the membrane surface in a permeable layer that adds flow resistance.
facts.quote: Cake filtration occurs when particles accumulate on the surface of a membrane in a permeable cake of increasing thickness that adds resistance to flow.

facts.text: In the cake-complete model, cake forms on the area that remains unblocked, and blockage removes membrane area from flow.
facts.quote: Cake forms on the membrane area that is not blocked. Complete blockage can occur on portions of the membrane area where a cake has formed. There is no flux through blocked membrane area.

facts.text: The cake-complete model idealizes caking and complete blocking as independent effects, although the paper notes that they may interact in real filtration.
facts.quote: The combined cake-complete model idealizes fouling as occurring by the independent effect of complete blocking and caking.

The model uses two fitted parameters, one for cake filtration and one for complete blocking.
The combined fouling relations were derived using Darcy’s law.
facts.quote: Five new fouling models that accounted for the combined effects of the different individual fouling mechanisms were derived from Darcy's law.

bolton_2006_cake_intermediate_blocking.name: Cake-intermediate blocking
bolton_2006_cake_intermediate_blocking.description: The cake-intermediate blocking model describes fouling during filtration of biological fluids through microporous or virus-retention membranes. It predicts permeate volume over time during constant-pressure operation and pressure rise over time during constant-flow operation. The model combines loss of available membrane area through intermediate blocking with increasing flow resistance from cake formation, using Darcy’s law to derive explicit time-dependent equations. The authors evaluated it with human plasma IgG filtered through Durapore PVDF membranes and BSA filtered through Viresolve 180 membranes, under both constant-pressure and constant-flow conditions. They fitted two parameters by minimizing squared residuals and compared its predictions with individual and other combined fouling models.

bolton_2006_cake_standard_blocking.name: Cake-standard blocking
bolton_2006_cake_standard_blocking.description: The combined cake-standard blocking model describes fouling of a membrane by both cake formation on its surface and pore constriction within the membrane. It predicts filtered volume over time during constant-pressure operation and pressure over time during constant-flow operation, using Darcy’s law and the two mechanisms’ effects on filtration resistance. The model has two fitted parameters and is formulated with algebraic relations rather than dynamic state equations. The paper tested combined fouling models using human plasma IgG filtered through a sterilizing-grade PVDF membrane and BSA filtered through a virus-retention membrane, under both constant-pressure and constant-flow conditions. The cake-standard model improved fits in some tests, but the authors present it as most applicable when the observed fouling is consistent with both mechanisms, rather than as a model that fits a broad range of fouling curves.

facts.quote: In this case the available membrane area will not decline over the course of the run.

facts.text: The model treats cake formation and standard blocking as independent mechanisms that proceed throughout filtration.

bolton_2006_complete_standard_blocking.name: Complete-standard blocking
bolton_2006_complete_standard_blocking.description: The Complete-standard blocking model describes fouling during filtration of biological fluids through microporous membranes by combining complete pore blockage with standard blocking, in which deposits constrict pores. It predicts permeate volume over time at constant pressure and pressure over time at constant flow, using explicit relationships derived from Darcy’s law. The model has two fitted fouling parameters and is intended for cases where both mechanisms are relevant; it reduces to the corresponding single-mechanism model when one mechanism dominates. The paper compares its fits with individual fouling models using sterile filtration data for human plasma IgG and virus-filtration data for BSA, collected in small membrane holders. Across the reported comparisons, the combined model fit about as well as standard blocking alone, while other combined models performed better for some data sets. bolton_2006_intermediate_standard_blocki.description: The Intermediate-standard blocking model represents protein fouling of microporous membranes by combining intermediate blocking, which reduces the available pore area, with standard blocking, which constricts pores and raises filtration resistance. Based on Darcy’s law, it predicts filtrate volume over time during constant-pressure filtration and pressure rise over time during constant-flow filtration using two fitted parameters. The paper tested it on human IgG filtration through a 0.22 μm PVDF membrane and BSA filtration through a virus-retention membrane, including constant-pressure and constant-flow runs. Model curves were fitted to measured filtration profiles by minimizing the sum of squared residuals. In the tested cases, this combined model did not improve on the relevant individual blocking model, and the authors describe it as applicable when the combined mechanisms match observed fouling.

facts.text: Intermediate blocking represents some particles sealing pores while other deposited particles accumulate on top of them.
